newsitem.title: UK: Few passengers show up for first Eurostar trains.
newsitem.headline: Few passengers show up for first Eurostar trains.

text.p: Passengers were scarce on Wednesday aboard the first express trains to run through the Channel Tunnel since a fire last month injured 34 people and provoked intense concern over safety in the England-France rail link.

Train operator Eurostar resumed the passenger service between London and Paris and Brussels a few hours after safety officials said they were satisfied with evacuation procedures and safety equipment in the 51 km (32 mile) tunnel.
"This is the news we've all been waiting for. It's great to be back," Eurostar (UK) Ltd's deputy chairman, Adam Mills, said.
The tunnel has been closed to passenger traffic since November 18, when a fire on a truck destroyed a freight train, injuring 34 people and severely damaging a section of tunnel.
Late on Tuesday the Inter-Governmental Commission (IGC) of French and British government representatives said a limited passenger service could resume while repairs continued.

Only one of the two tunnels under the sea is being used. Freight traffic resumed a few days after the fire and passenger vehicle shuttles are due from on December 10. Freight vehicle shuttles of the type where the fire occurred will only resume after a French investigation of the accident is over.
Just a few passengers boarded the first trains to leave London's Waterloo station for Paris and Brussels, Eurostar said.
"There were very few," a spokeswoman said. "We didn't get the go-ahead from the IGC until late yesterday afternoon."
The spokeswoman said she had no numbers but said bookings were picking up as passengers heard the tunnel was open.
Eurostar it said it would resume 90 percent of its normal services, with 13 trains per day to Paris and seven to Brussels.
The damaged tunnel remains closed while it undergoes extensive repairs from the fire, which burned cables and buckled track. Trains will alternate through the remaining tunnel.
Tunnel operator Eurotunnel SA Plc ran a drill on Sunday to prove it could safely run passenger services.
But Ken Cameron of Britain's Fire Brigades Union said he had serious questions about the tunnel's safety.

"Here we are within two weeks of a major fire, where we have got a construction site operating in the tunnel, which is going to cause tremendous problems of congestion, or of the accidents that do happen on building sites," he told BBC radio.

Cameron said an escape tunnel meant for evacuating passengers was still damaged, adding that Sunday's drill had not reassured him. "I think that was an absolute exercise in public relations rather than safety," he said.

"The fact that the (strickened) train didn't uncouple, the fact that evacuation of smoke did not take place, the fact that the train was not able to carry on out of the tunnel -- all of these things have not been answered, yet we're putting Eurostar down there today with hundreds of people on board."
But Mills said the company had been assured the tunnel was safe. "We certainly would never do anything which would prejudice the safety of our Eurostar passengers," he told BBC.
Passengers expressed no fears. "After an incident like this it's probably safer because they are trying so hard," one woman said as she boarded an early train.
"If they are allowing passengers through my assumption is it's relatively safe. It's certainly safer than flying," a male passenger told Sky television.

A pair of Japanese tourists boarding a Paris-bound train expressed delight at having a choice of seats on the normally crowded service. Shares in Eurotunnel strengthened in London 1.5p to 82p on news of the resumption in passenger services. ($1=.5995 Pound)
